Definition: Whether the country has established policies, regulations, and programmes supporting off-grid and distributed energy solutions (mini-grids, solar home systems). These are critical for extending ICT infrastructure to unserved areas beyond the central grid.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original row scored 0/Unknown with no source cited. A single light Exa check surfaced clearly authoritative government policy documents, so the row was moved from the fast path to the full verification path. Fetched the Ministry of Energy and Public Utilities' Energy and Water Strategy 2024-2027, the Renewable Energy Roadmap 2030, and DLA Piper's 2022 Africa Energy Futures legal review, plus the Electricity Act 2005. These confirm a comprehensive distributed/renewable energy policy framework: the MARENA Act 2015 created a dedicated renewable energy agency; active schemes include the Net Billing Solar PV Scheme, the Home Solar Project for low-income households, dedicated schemes for religious bodies and NGOs, and the Medium Scale Distributed Generation Scheme with a feed-in tariff; measured deployment includes 32MW of rooftop solar installed by April 2024 and 104MW of industrial interconnection agreements under the Carbon Neutral Industrial Sector scheme as at May 2024. Score revised from 0 (Unknown) to 4 (Comprehensive framework with significant deployment). Note that this variable's definition is oriented toward off-grid mini-grids for unserved rural areas; Mauritius has near-universal grid electrification, so classic isolated off-grid mini-grids are largely inapplicable, but grid-connected distributed generation/solar home system policy is comprehensively documented and substantially deployed, supporting a 4 rather than the off-grid-specific ceiling of 5.
revised_comments: Mauritius has a comprehensive distributed and renewable energy policy framework overseen by the Mauritius Renewable Energy Agency (MARENA), established under the MARENA Act 2015. Distributed generation is actively supported through the Net Billing Solar PV Scheme (eligibility threshold raised to 300kW consumption in January 2024), the Home Solar Project providing subsidised rooftop solar kits to low-income households (around 2,000 installations completed by April 2024 of a planned 5,000), dedicated schemes for religious bodies and NGOs, and the Medium Scale Distributed Generation Scheme with a feed-in tariff of Rs4.20 per kWh. The Carbon Neutral Industrial Sector Renewable Energy Scheme has signed interconnection agreements covering 104MW of industrial capacity as of May 2024. Fiscal incentives, including capital allowances, VAT zero-rating on photovoltaic equipment, and tax deductions for household solar investment, support uptake. Around 32MW of rooftop solar PV had been installed on residential and non-residential buildings by April 2024, alongside a 20MW battery energy storage system at Amaury commissioned to help the grid absorb distributed renewable generation. The framework is set out in the Ministry of Energy and Public Utilities' Energy and Water Strategy 2024-2027 and the Renewable Energy Roadmap 2030.

Definition: Frequency and severity of power outages experienced by businesses and households. Based on World Bank Enterprise Surveys, Afrobarometer, or national utility data. Reflects the quality of electricity supply beyond mere access — critical for running ICT equipment and data infrastructure.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original row scored 0/Unknown with no source. A single light Exa check surfaced the World Bank Enterprise Survey (WBES) 2023 for Mauritius with directly relevant outage microdata, so the row was moved from the fast path to the full verification path. Fetched the WBES 2023 study description and the variable-level data dictionaries for outage incidence (c6) and outages per typical month (c7). Raw microdata (fieldwork May 2023-February 2024, n=353 firms): 41.6% of firms (147/353) reported at least one power outage in the last fiscal year; among those reporting a frequency, the modal value is one outage per month (51 of 136 valid responses), with a long tail up to 31 per month, giving an unofficial unweighted mean of roughly 1.1 outages/month across all firms but a median of 0 (i.e. most firms had none). The official WDI aggregate indicator (IC.ELC.OUTG, power outages in a typical month) has been discontinued on the World Bank Data portal and could not be retrieved as a single published country figure, so this assessment rests on calculation from raw microdata rather than an official published aggregate. Given the scale thresholds (3=monthly/occasional disruptions, 4=rare outages <10/year) sit close to this data (implied ~13 outages/year on the mean, but median 0), the classification is genuinely borderline between 3 and 4. Scored 3 (Moderate) as the more conservative reading given roughly 42% of firms experienced recurring monthly-type outages, but flagged for human review because no single authoritative published aggregate figure was found and the categorisation required interpretive judgement on raw survey microdata.
revised_comments: Mauritius's grid reliability is assessed using the World Bank Enterprise Survey 2023 (fieldwork May 2023 to February 2024). Of 353 surveyed formal-sector firms, 41.6% reported experiencing at least one power outage during the last fiscal year, while 58.4% reported none. Among firms that did experience outages, the most commonly reported frequency was one outage per month, with a small number of firms reporting higher frequencies of up to several per month. This points to an electricity supply with occasional, generally monthly-scale disruptions for a substantial minority of firms, rather than severe or frequent (weekly or daily) outages, consistent with a grid undergoing active modernisation, including underground cabling, smart meter rollout, and a 20MW battery energy storage system commissioned in 2024 to help manage peak demand and grid stability.
